what_it_does: RowHammer is a hardware vulnerability in modern RAM chips: repeatedly reading from one row of memory cells causes electrical disturbance in neighboring rows, which can randomly flip bits in those neighbors — potentially corrupting data or allowing a hacker to escalate privileges. Defenses against RowHammer work by tracking how many times each row has been accessed, and issuing a protective refresh of vulnerable neighboring rows before bit flips can occur. These trackers often use shared counting structures, and this paper identifies a new threat: an attacker can study how the tracker's shared mapping works, then deliberately access rows in a pattern that inflates the counts of rows belonging to other (innocent) programs, triggering unnecessary refreshes that slow those programs down — a so-called Performance Attack. DAPPER defeats this by randomizing which row maps to which slot in the tracker using cryptographic hashing, so an attacker cannot predict or manipulate counter assignments. An enhanced version uses double-hashing and piggybacks protective refreshes onto the scheduled periodic refresh operations that RAM already requires, keeping overhead low. The design uses only 96 KB of fast on-chip memory (called SRAM) per 32 GB of main RAM.
